title: Molten Aluminum-Induced Corrosion and Wear-Resistance Properties of ZrB<sub>2</sub>-Based Cermets Improved by Sintering-Temperature Manipulation.

recollection.starting_material: ZrB2-based cermet powder with minor additions of metallic binder (e.g., Ni or Co) and sintering aids
recollection.intervention: Systematic variation of sintering temperature in a hot-press or spark-plasma-sintering process between ~1600 °C and ~1900 °C
recollection.structure: Densified ZrB2 grains reinforced by a network of finely distributed metallic binder and in situ-formed secondary boride phases (e.g., ZrC, WB) at optimal sintering temperature
recollection.mechanism: Higher sintering temperature promotes liquid-phase sintering of the metallic binder, improved densification, refined grain boundaries, and enhanced formation of protective oxide layers at the cermet/melt interface, which together mitigate molten-Al attack and adhesive wear
recollection.results: At the optimized sintering temperature (~1800 °C), the cermet showed a corrosion rate in molten Al of ~0.05 mm/y (versus ~0.15 mm/y at 1600 °C) and a wear rate under sliding tests of ~1.2×10⁻⁶ mm³/N·m (versus ~4.5×10⁻⁶ mm³/N·m at the lowest temperature)

score.note: The recollection correctly identifies sintering-temperature variation and broadly invokes liquid-phase densification by a metallic binder, but gives the wrong temperature range and optimum (actual: SPS at 1300–1600 °C, optimum 1500 °C). The binder-filled compact structure is only partly captured; the claimed secondary borides and protective oxide mechanism are unsupported. Reported corrosion and wear metrics use incorrect values and units and omit the actual density, hardness, toughness, corrosion-rate, wear-volume, and friction-coefficient results.
